newsitem.title: SPAIN: Belgrade leaders seek Spanish aid to rebuild city.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade leaders seek Spanish aid to rebuild city.

text.p: Belgrade's newly-recognised leaders launched a marketing road trip in Spain on Tuesday to drum up foreign aid for the crumbling city, which they said was depleted of funds and hamstrung by the ruling Socialists.

The opposition's three-party coalition Zajedno (Together) assumed control of the city last week after three months of mass street protests forced Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to recognise Zajedno's electoral victory.
"We have taken the first step toward democracy in Serbia but there is still much to do," Vesna Pesic, Civic Alliance party chief and Zajedno co-leader, told a news conference in Madrid.
"We are very satisfied with the Spanish government's offer of help...I am confident Spain's other political parties will also support our programme of aid."

Spain will send teams of specialists to rebuild Belgrade's infrastructure, in addition to providing equipment like buses and medical supplies, Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said after meeting the three Zajedno leaders.
He did not specify the amount of the offer.

"The city is in a total state of ruin and we are in favour of offering cooperation, the same as other European countries are doing," he said. "We all have a vested interest in seeing Serbia, the spinal column of the Balkans, achieve peace."
Analysts in the former Yugoslavia have warned the climate created by the protests could lead to social and economic unrest against both Milosevic and the newly installed opposition parties.
A pressing concern for Zajedno is that Milosevic will use Socialist control of state industries and central government to strangle the city by denying financial aid and services.

"The Socialist party has done everything it can to block work in the city and it will do more," Belgrade mayor and Zajedno co-leader Zoran Djindjic said. "We see many problems when Milosevic puts sanctions on Belgrade."
The Zajedno leaders, who are to visit London next, said they were seeking foreign help to compensate for a potential lack of central government assistance.

While Djindjic admitted there was a learning curve as the Zajedno leaders started on the difficult task of moving from a street protest movement to city hall management, co-leader Vuk Draskovic dismissed foreign media reports of a growing split in the coalition.

"We are sorry to disappoint you, but we are very united, very strong and we have signed a document of common aims, a common programme for now as well as for the presidential elections," Draskovic told the news conference.
Analysts have warned that Milosevic will exploit any sign of weakness within the coalition, which is planning to challenge the Socialists in parliamentary elections this year.

Draskovic defined the coalition's platform as trying to establish European systems in Serbia for democracy, parliament, the economy and markets, while creating independent media and courts and a non-ideological army and police force.
"We would like to see Europe in Serbia not Serbia in Europe," Draskovic said.

Later on Tuesday, the Zajedno leaders met Spain's former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, whom they thanked for heading an election investigation mission by Europe's security body OSCE that declared the opposition's victory valid.
They were also to meet the leader of the United Left coalition and representatives of the other political parties.
